name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Thursday 25 January 1973

clue.text: Sport made by Potter

blocks.note: first meaning: the game played by rolling woods towards a jack on a green
second meaning: round dishes thrown on a wheel by a potter

explanation.surface: A game invented by someone called Potter.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P makes Potter look like a person's name; it is just someone who makes pottery.
explanation.definitionFit: The lawn game is named in the plural, and the same word names the deep round dishes a ceramicist shapes from clay.

clue.text: Une mauvaise demi minute over fashion in Gloucestershire?

definitions.note: the answer is a place found there, so the phrase stands for the place

indicators.note: demi is French for half, so only the opening half of the following word is kept

blocks.note: French for a bad one; mauvaise translates as bad
the first half of minute, also its usual abbreviation
ton means the prevailing fashion or style

explanation.surface: A bad half-minute, told in French, somewhere in an English county.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' just means the first pieces sit above the last one. Badminton is a village and estate in Gloucestershire, home of the horse trials.
explanation.definitionFit: The village and great house of the Dukes of Beaufort lie in that county, and gave their name to the shuttlecock game.

clue.text: Look out! It may be the dog?

blocks.note: first meaning: be on guard, keep a lookout
second meaning: a dog kept to guard property is called by this word plus dog

explanation.surface: A warning shout about a dangerous dog.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep guard is to look out, and a guard dog is a watchdog, so the word can be the dog's job.

clue.text: b retired last year

blocks.note: surface reading: something labelled b went into retirement recently
setter's reading: a pre-decimal coin, written with a single-letter abbreviation, withdrawn when the currency went decimal

explanation.surface: Someone or something called b stepped down a year ago.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'b' is probably a misprint for 's', the old abbreviation for the coin worth twelve pence, which disappeared with decimal currency.
explanation.definitionFit: The coin worth twelve pennies was abbreviated with one letter and taken out of use when Britain and Australia switched to decimal money.

clue.text: Practised in court to give the lad a calling?

definitions.note: a past-tense verb phrase, like the answer
the answer is the past tense, 'gave a call'

blocks.note: first meaning: warmed up on a tennis court before a match
second meaning: woke someone by rapping on the door, as a knocker-up once did

explanation.surface: Practising law in court as a way of giving a young man a vocation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' and 'calling' suggest the law as a profession; the court is a tennis court and the calling is a wake-up knock. In Britain a knocker-up was paid to wake workers.
explanation.definitionFit: A pre-match rally is a knock-up, and to rouse a sleeper by knocking is the older British sense of the same phrasal verb.

clue.text: Hang on to the stronghold

blocks.note: first meaning: retain, not give up
second meaning: the central tower of a castle

explanation.surface: Keep your grip on the fortress.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means retain possession, and as a noun it names the inner fortified tower of a medieval castle.

clue.text: Officiating as a judge of form?

definitions.note: a form is a long seat, so the phrase means seated on one

blocks.note: first meaning: serving as a magistrate or judge, whose seat of office is the bench
second meaning: a form is a backless bench, so this is sitting on that kind of seat

explanation.surface: Acting as someone who judges how good a performance is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judge of form' sounds like a racing tipster; form here is the old word for a long wooden seat.
explanation.definitionFit: Judges sit on the bench as their seat of office, and a form is literally a bench, so the phrase covers both.

clue.text: One in a hundred in trouble with decapitation

definitions.text: One in a hundred in trouble with decapitation

blocks.clueFragment: One in a hundred in trouble
blocks.note: surface reading: a rare person who has got into difficulties and lost their head
setter's reading: remove the first letter of trouble to leave a Russian currency, and the answer is one hundredth of it

explanation.surface: A rare individual in serious trouble, facing the executioner.
explanation.walkthrough: Behead 'trouble' and you are left with the Russian rouble; the answer is the coin worth a hundredth of a rouble.
explanation.definitionFit: A Russian coin worth one hundredth part of a rouble, as a cent is of a dollar.

clue.text: Fitting to provide diversion of course

definitions.text: Fitting to provide diversion of course

blocks.clueFragment: Fitting to provide diversion of course
blocks.note: surface reading: naturally it is appropriate to offer some entertainment

blocks.clueFragment: Fitting to provide diversion of course
blocks.note: setter's reading: a piece of equipment that turns something away from its path

explanation.surface: Of course it is right to lay on some amusement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fitting' looks like an adjective (appropriate) and 'diversion' like entertainment; read as a noun, it is a device that changes the course of a flow.
explanation.definitionFit: A plate or vane fitted to turn air, water or projectiles aside changes their course, which is exactly a diversion.

clue.text: Jobs for the supporters

blocks.note: first meaning: positions of employment
second meaning: upright poles that hold something up

explanation.surface: Work found for a team's fans.
explanation.definitionFit: Appointments to employment are called this, and so are the upright timbers that hold up a fence or a goal crossbar.

clue.text: Without unusual merit, depression causes harm

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the normal order, so these letters are rearranged
without in its old sense means outside, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: a dent is a small hollow pressed into a surface
the five letters of merit, reshuffled

explanation.surface: Lacking any special merit, feeling low does you damage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking' but is the old sense of 'outside', so the depression wraps around the jumbled merit.
explanation.definitionFit: Detriment is damage or loss suffered, the same noun as harm in phrases like 'to the harm of'.

clue.text: Delicacies of the Big Bad Wolf's demolition method

definitions.text: the Big Bad Wolf's demolition method

blocks.note: first meaning: light pastries, such as cream ones

blocks.clueFragment: the Big Bad Wolf's demolition method
blocks.note: second meaning: the wolf in the Three Little Pigs huffs and blows the houses down

explanation.surface: Fancy food tied to how the wolf flattened the pigs' houses.
explanation.definitionFit: Light hollow pastries filled with cream are named this, and the wolf brought the houses down with breaths of air.

clue.text: Have an inspiration

blocks.note: surface reading: get a sudden bright idea
setter's reading: inspiration in its literal sense is drawing air into the lungs

explanation.walkthrough: Inspiration's literal, medical sense is breathing in, which is what the verb means.
explanation.definitionFit: Inspiration literally means drawing breath into the lungs, so to have one is simply to breathe in.

clue.text: Cheers at assembly for those who impart know-ledge

indicators.note: things put together at an assembly are arranged afresh, so these letters are rebuilt

blocks.note: all eight letters, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Applause at the school assembly for the staff who teach.
explanation.walkthrough: School assembly is exactly where teachers are found, so the surface hides the indicator in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: The people who pass on knowledge in a classroom are its staff, described by what they do.

clue.text: Take good care of the bail 11 in the Scottish league

definitions.note: the answer is a club in that league

blocks.note: first meaning: to look after someone tenderly, as a parent would, is to treat them in this way
second meaning: a football club from Lanarkshire

explanation.surface: Look after a player in Scottish football.
explanation.walkthrough: The words 'the bail 11' look garbled in the printed clue and add nothing usable. Motherwell is a Scottish town and its football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as a phrase it means nurture someone well, and as one word it names a Scottish town whose football club plays in the national league.

clue.text: Sort of £500 note used in place of the real stuff

definitions.text: used in place of the real stuff

indicators.note: to sort is to rearrange, so the words that follow are put into another order

blocks.note: monkey is British slang for five hundred pounds
taken as written

explanation.surface: A kind of five-hundred-pound banknote passed off as genuine currency.
explanation.walkthrough: A monkey is British slang for £500; its letters with 'note' rearrange into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Coins or vouchers whose face value exceeds their worth stand in for proper currency, which is what the phrase describes.

clue.text: Sharp advantage in a delicate situation

blocks.note: first meaning: the keen cutting rim of a blade, an edge in both senses
second meaning: a precarious state where things could go either way

explanation.surface: A slight lead held in a tricky position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Advantage' plays on edge meaning a lead; the blade's sharp rim is the literal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The thin cutting line of a blade is literal, and being balanced on one is the idiom for a precarious, finely poised state.

clue.text: Cheek at the front of the ship

definitions.note: almost certainly a misprint for 'Check', a verb like the answer

blocks.note: first meaning, reading the printed word as 'Check': hold back or stop a flow
second meaning: the upright timber at the bow

explanation.surface: Insolence shown at a ship's bow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheek' gives nothing; read it as 'Check', which is surely what was meant.
explanation.definitionFit: To stem a flow is to check it, and the curved timber rising at the bow of a vessel has the same name.

clue.text: Being wide-awake for example on Brown Island

blocks.note: a human being
a wide-awake is a soft broad-brimmed felt hat
tan is a light brown

explanation.surface: Staying alert, such as on an island called Brown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wide-awake' looks like alertness but is a kind of soft felt hat, so 'for example' marks it as one instance of a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: The borough at the heart of New York City sits on its own island between the Hudson and East rivers.

clue.text: Whistle stop and start men

blocks.note: surface reading: a brief halt by a train at a small station
setter's reading: officials who blow a whistle to halt and restart play

explanation.surface: Men who start and stop on a whistle-stop train tour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whistle stop' looks like the railway phrase; split it and it describes match officials blowing to stop and start the game.
explanation.definitionFit: Match officials in football and rugby blow a whistle to halt play and to restart it.

clue.text: "And Dick the shepherd blows his (L. L. Lost)

blocks.note: surface reading: an unfinished line about a shepherd blowing something
setter's reading: the line is from the winter song in Love's Labour's Lost, completed by the missing word

explanation.walkthrough: The winter song ending Shakespeare's Love's Labour's Lost has the shepherd blowing on his fingertip to warm it: the missing word ends the line.
explanation.definitionFit: In the song the cold shepherd blows on his fingernail to warm his hands, so the word completes the quotation.

clue.text: One for the birds, faint hearted and single?

blocks.note: chicken means cowardly
in cricket a single is one run

explanation.surface: A timid, unmarried person is dismissed as hopeless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For the birds' sounds like slang for worthless, but it is literal: a place for hens.
explanation.definitionFit: A fenced enclosure where poultry are kept is built for birds, which is what the phrase describes.

clue.text: In a time of prosperity many are flowering

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other, so the later word sits within the earlier phrase

blocks.note: taken as written
a boom is a period of rapid economic growth
L is the Roman numeral for fifty, a crossword stand-in for many

explanation.surface: When times are good, lots of plants bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like the start of a time phrase, but it tells you to put the numeral inside the phrase before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Plants in bloom are in flower, and this adjective is the predicative form of that state.

clue.text: One is not bound to start life thus

definitions.text: One is not bound to start life thus

blocks.note: not tied up or enslaved
to be born is to begin life

explanation.surface: Nobody is forced to begin their life in this way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not bound to' looks like 'not obliged to'; read literally it means free of bonds, and the whole clue also defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone whose birth was to free parents rather than in slavery or serfdom began life without bonds of servitude.

clue.text: This rate wins the race

blocks.note: surface reading: a speed fast enough to win
setter's reading: the word that comes before rate to mean excellent, and the place of the winner

explanation.surface: Run at this speed and you win.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rate' looks like speed; joined to the answer it makes the phrase for top quality, and the answer alone is the winning position.
explanation.definitionFit: The top position in a race belongs to the winner, and with 'rate' added the word means of the highest quality.

clue.text: Hamlet's mobled queen

blocks.note: surface reading: Hamlet's mother, Gertrude, the queen of Denmark
setter's reading: the player's speech in Hamlet describes the veiled queen of Troy

explanation.walkthrough: The queen of Hamlet is Gertrude, but 'the mobled queen' is a line from the player's speech about the fall of Troy, describing Priam's wife.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hamlet the player recites the grief of the Trojan queen, muffled in a veil, and Hamlet repeats 'the mobled queen'.

clue.text: Make vertical cocktail for instance

blocks.note: first meaning: stand something on its end
second meaning: to cock a tail is to turn its end upward

explanation.surface: Tip a cocktail glass upright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cocktail' looks like a drink; read as cock + tail, it is turning a tail upward.
explanation.definitionFit: To set an object on its end is to stand it up, and cocking a tail raises the end of it.

clue.text: Jug of Punch

definitions.note: the answer is the dog belonging to Punch

blocks.note: first meaning: a beer mug shaped like a seated man in a tricorn hat
second meaning: the dog in the Punch and Judy puppet show

explanation.surface: A jug full of punch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Punch' looks like the drink; it is the puppet, whose dog has this name.
explanation.definitionFit: A pottery beer mug modelled as a stout man is named this, and so is the dog in the Punch and Judy show.

clue.text: Extra diode needed to demonstrate wireless

indicators.note: to demonstrate is to show, so the answer is on display within the clue words

blocks.note: found across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: An additional diode is required to show off a wireless set.
explanation.walkthrough: A diode is a real radio part, so the surface makes sense as electronics.
explanation.definitionFit: Wireless is the older British word for a broadcast receiver set.

clue.text: Escape to voluntary bondage?

blocks.note: surface reading: fleeing into a slavery one chooses
setter's reading: marriage, a tie entered freely, reached by running away with a lover

explanation.walkthrough: The 'bondage' is the marriage tie, and the escape is running off to wed in secret.
explanation.definitionFit: Couples who run away secretly to marry escape from their families into wedlock, a bond they choose.

clue.text: How hot air rises!

blocks.note: surface reading: a question or exclamation about warm air going up
setter's reading: an adverb describing upward movement by warm currents

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation reads as a remark about boasting; the answer is the adverb from warm rising currents.
explanation.definitionFit: Warm air goes up in columns called thermals, so it ascends by means of heat, which the adverb describes.

clue.text: A battle between two chairmen

blocks.note: first meaning: the 1870 battle in which Napoleon III was captured by the Prussians
second meaning: a covered chair carried on poles by two bearers, known as chairmen

explanation.surface: A fight between two company chairmen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chairmen' suggests boardrooms; the old chairmen were porters who carried a passenger in an enclosed chair.
explanation.definitionFit: A French town gave its name to the 1870 battle, and also to the enclosed chair carried by a pair of bearers.
